  • Look at the list of the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, and you’ll see more than just a parade of billionaires with good taste (or at least expensive taste).
  • Yes, Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million, but is it really a Leonardo?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Auction records make for great headlines, like the 2026 banner sale of Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which topped $236.4 million at Sotheby’s. There’s a thrill in watching numbers climb into the stratosphere, each sale another reminder that, in the art market, money has a way of bending reality. But the price of a painting has never been the most interesting thing about it.

Look at the list of the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, and you’ll see more than just a parade of billionaires with good taste (or at least expensive taste). You’ll see a history of ideas—what mattered to the artists who made them, what obsessed the collectors who chased them, and how we decide, decades or centuries later, which works still hold power.

Yes, Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million, but is it really a Leonardo? Picasso’s Women of Algiers, Pollock’s Number 7A, 1948, and Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn all shattered records, with the Pollock work shooting far beyond its $100 million estimate when it came to auction at Christie’s in May 2026 in a sale of works from the S. I. Newhouse collection. But these works’ real value has nothing to do with what someone was willing to pay on a given evening at Christie’s. The best art—the kind that shifts culture, lingers in your mind, and changes how you see the world—exists in a space money can’t touch.

It has been revealed that but of course, once a work crosses a threshold, there’s something almost inevitable about the price spiral. With each record-breaking sale, the bar gets set higher, the stakes get sharper, and the frenzy deepens. The game has changed, but in a way, the auction houses are just as much a stage for the spectacle as for the art itself. Every price tag opens the door to another possibility. If one work can sell for $450 million, what’s to stop the next from reaching half a billion—or more? With so many players in the game, all vying for the ultimate cultural trophy, the numbers have a way of multiplying faster than the logic behind them.

According to recent reports, and yet, the more those numbers rise, the further they drift from the essential thing that makes art so valuable: the art itself. High prices can make us think we’re in the presence of something transcendent, but it’s the work that holds the power, not the price. So, here’s the list. The numbers are staggering, but don’t get too caught up in them. The real story is in the art itself.

Industry observers note that A version of this article was first published on November 19, 2025. It was last updated on November 20, 2026.

Sold for $119.9 million at Sotheby’s New York in May 2012.

When it sold for $107 million at Sotheby’s Upcoming York, Munch’s pastel The Scream (1895), one of the four versions—two painted and two in pastel—that he made of the same subject, became the most expensive work ever to be sold at a public auction, stealing the trophy from Picasso’s 1932 Nude, Green Leaves and Bust, which sold at Christie’s in 2010 for $106.5 million.

At the time, it was the only version of The Scream still in private hands; its seller was Petter Olsen, a Norwegian businessman whose father, Thomas, was Munch’s friend and patron. The picture, which opened at $40 million, sparked a 12-minute bidding war, with wide-eyed potential buyers both in the salesroom and on the phones. According to the Wall Street Journal, its buyer was investor Leon Black, a trustee at the Museum of Modern Art, where The Scream later went on view.

After the sale Olsen, described by Art in America as “the wild-haired and bespectacled seller,” read a statement that tied the work to climate change and global warming: “The Scream for me shows the horrifying moment when man realizes his impact on nature and the irreversible changes that he has initiated, making the planet increasingly uninhabitable. . . . More death, less life. And very few lifeboats left as we go down.”.

Sold for $121 million at Christie’s Upcoming York in November 2024.

According to recent reports, the “crown jewel” of the auction market in 2024 (as Christie’s so humbly put it) was perhaps the finest example of a subject that Magritte revisited more than 25 times throughout his career: an otherworldly scene showing a house on tree-lined street at night. But instead being enveloped in darkness, the sky above the trees is impossibly blue, with major, cottony clouds floating by. This 1954 version of Empire of Light, which sold for $121 million and came from the collection of designer and philanthropist Mica Ertegun, set a new record for Magritte’s work at auction.

Recent findings suggest that after the sale, Christie’s chairman of 20th and 21st century art Alex Rotter stated the house that evening had adopted a “masterpiece approach” to this sale. “In a market that is not so easy to maneuver, we thought that if we present the greatest works we can get … these are the best examples,” Rotter said, admitting that the auction had its share of lots that didn’t catch collectors’ attention. But “the works that we put all the emphasis behind really proved us right. They had multiple bidders and revealed that a market based on individual taste is on the rise.”.

Sold for $137.7 million at Christie’s New York in November 2022.

It has been revealed that cézanne’s deliciously rich landscape of the French countryside and his beloved Mont Sainte-Victoire is the second of five works from the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s to make this list. When the hammer fell, Mont Sainte-Victoire (1888–90) doubled Cézanne’s previous auction high of $60.5 million, for a still life from the collection of John Hay Whitney.

In a recent development, like Cézanne’s best works, Mont Sainte-Victoire breaks aspects of the world—in this case, a French mountain—into shapes shaded with color, as though they were three-dimensional geometrical forms. In that way, Cézanne paved the way for Cubist artists such as Pablo Picasso and George Braque, who would push his innovations even further toward abstraction.

Sold for $139.3 million at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in November 2023.

Woman with a Watch (1932), one of Picasso’s many paintings of his mistress Marie-Thérèse Walter, became the second most expensive work by the artist ever sold at auction when it fetched $139 million at Sotheby’s in 2023. The canvas, from the collection of late philanthropist Emily Fisher Landau, drew intense bidding before selling to a phone bidder represented by Sotheby’s head of global fine art, Brooke Lampley.

Woman with a Watch had a rarefied provenance, changing hands just a few times since Picasso painted it in 1932. It was acquired by Landau in 1968 from Pace Gallery, which had purchased it from Switzerland’s Galerie Beyeler two years earlier.

Sources indicate that pictures of Walter typically go for top dollar. In 2010, Nude, Green Leaves and Bust—also painted in 1932—broke records at $106.5 million. Still, the most expensive Picasso of all time is a work that does not depict Walter. But more on that in a bit.

Sold for $140.8 million at Poly International Auction Co., Ltd., Beijing in December 2017.

Qi Baishi’s Twelve Screens of Landscapes (1925) shattered records in 2017, selling for RMB 931.5 million ($140.8 million) at Beijing Poly Auction and making it the most expensive Chinese artwork ever sold at auction. The bidding war lasted over 20 minutes, with more than 60 bid increments before a Chinese collector secured the 12-panel piece.

According to recent reports, each 70-inch panel captures a sweeping vista from Qi’s travels across China. Originally displayed at his solo exhibition in 1954 and later featured in a memorial show in 1958, the set of panels was kept by Qi’s pupil, Xiuyi Guo, before resurfacing at auction.

A similar version of Twelve Screens of Landscapes, painted around 1932 as a gift to Kuomintang general Wang Zuanxu, resides in the Chongqing Museum. The set sold in 2017 was the only one in private hands at the time, making it a rarity.

Sold for $141.3 million at Christie’s Upcoming York in May 2015.

Recent findings suggest that alberto Giacometti’s Pointing Man (1947) became the most expensive sculpture ever sold at auction when it fetched $141.3 million at Christie’s Latest York in May 2015. The life-size bronze, standing at more than five and a half feet tall, was sold by real estate magnate Sheldon Solow, surpassing Giacometti’s previous auction record of $104.3 million, which was set at Sotheby’s London five years earlier by Walking Man I (1960).

One of six casts made by the artist (not counting an additional artist’s proof), this particular Pointing Man had been held privately for 45 years before the sale. Four of those casts reside in major museums, including the Museum of Modern Art in Upcoming York and the Tate in London, which made this auction a prime opportunity for collectors. Similar sculptures by Giacometti depicting skeletal, elongated figures have likewise sold for big sums.

At the time, Christie’s head Pylkkänen called the piece “one of the finest works of art I have had the honor to handle.” Whoever bought the piece clearly agreed about its quality.

Sold for $142.4 million at Christie’s New York in November 2013.

In a recent development, francis Bacon’s Three Studies of Lucian Freud (1969) briefly became the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction when it sold for $142.4 million at Christie’s Upcoming York in November 2013. The triptych surpassed the previous record, held by Edvard Munch’s pastel The Scream, which sold for $119.9 million at Sotheby’s in 2012 (and which also appears on this list, above).

Sources indicate that bacon’s three-panel portrait—each part stands six and a half feet tall—depicts Bacon’s longtime friend and artistic rival, Lucian Freud, in a series of contorted poses. The piece had an unusual history: its panels were separated by a dealer in the 1970s and remained apart for 15 years before being reunited by a collector in 1989.

Sources indicate that the work was expected to sell for over $85 million, but after a five-minute bidding war, it was secured by New York’s Acquavella Galleries. In a strategic move, Christie’s shifted the Bacon painting to the ninth lot of the evening to allow unsuccessful bidders a chance at other works—an approach that proved successful, contributing to the auction house’s record-breaking $691.6 million total for the night.

Shortly after the sale, the anonymous buyer lent the triptych to the Portland Art Museum for public viewing from December 2013 to March 2014.

Sold for $149 million at Christie’s New York in November 2022.

In a recent development, in November 2022, an early 20th-century masterpiece by Georges Seurat, Models (Small Version) (1888), sold for a staggering $149 million at Christie’s Newly introduced York. The painting, depicting three nude figures in Seurat’s signature pointillist style, was one of the rarest privately-owned works by the artist. It came from the collection of Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen and was expected to surpass $100 million at auction.

The bidding opened at $75 million, drawing competition from four bidders, including specialists representing clients in Upcoming York and Asia. After several minutes of heated back-and-forth, the work hammered at $130 million, with Christie’s Asia chairman securing the piece for a final total of $149 million, including fees. The sale set a new auction record for Seurat, shattering his previous high of $34 million, achieved in 2018 for The Harbor at Grandcamp(1885).

The last time Models (Small Version) appeared on the market was in 1970, when it fetched just over $1 million at Christie’s. Prior to Allen’s ownership, it had belonged to the influential collector John Quinn, a champion of modernist artists in the early 20th century.

Sold for $157.2 million at Sotheby’s New York in May 2018.

Recent findings suggest that amedeo Modigliani’s Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side) (1917), one of the artist’s most celebrated nudes, sold for $157.2 million at Sotheby’s New York in 2018. The total price, including the buyer’s premium, followed a hammer bid of $139 million, which fell just short of its undisclosed estimate of $150 million. Despite this, the sale set a record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at Sotheby’s at the time.

The large-scale canvas—depicting a nude woman gazing over her shoulder at the viewer—was the star lot of the auction house’s Impressionist and Modern art sale. Bidding opened at $125 million with auctioneer Helena Newman presiding over the room. The winning bid came from a client on the phone with Simon Shaw, Sotheby’s co-head of Impressionist and Modern art worldwide, after a subdued and measured exchange.

The work belongs to Modigliani’s groundbreaking series of reclining nudes, painted between 1916 and 1919. When first exhibited in 1917 at Parisian dealer Berthe Weill’s gallery, these erotic paintings caused such a scandal that police shut down the show after just two days. At the time, only two drawings were sold.

In a recent development, while the sale price was extraordinary, it did not surpass Modigliani’s auction record, which remains with Reclining Nude (1917–18), sold at Christie’s in 2015 for $170.4 million to Chinese collector Liu Yiqian. Sotheby’s, however, positioned Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side) as a transformative work, with Simon Shaw stating, “There is the nude before Modigliani, and there is the nude after Modigliani.”.

Sold for $170.4 million at Christie’s New York in November 2015.

Recent findings suggest that amedeo Modigliani’s Reclining Nude (1917–18) shattered expectations at Christie’s Fresh York in 2015, selling for $170.4 million, more than doubling the artist’s previous auction record of $70.7 million. The work, which carried an on-request estimate of over $100 million, became the second-most expensive painting ever sold at auction at the time.

It has been revealed that the sale took place during Christie’s curated evening auction, “The Artist’s Muse,” which aimed to build buzz around 20th-century masterpieces. Despite a mixed night—with several major lots, including works by Willem de Kooning and Lucian Freud, failing to sell—the Modigliani nude electrified the room. Bidding was fierce, ultimately concluding with a Chinese collector securing the work via telephone, as revealed by Pylkkänen after the sale. (The collector was later revealed to be Chinese billionaire businessman Liu Yiqian.).

Reclining Nude is part of Modigliani’s celebrated series of reclining nudes, painted between 1916 and 1919. These works, revolutionary in their sensuality and bold in their approach to form, scandalized Paris when first exhibited at Berthe Weill’s gallery in 1917, leading to the show’s abrupt closure by police. Today, they are considered among the most important contributions to the modern nude tradition.

The sale of Reclining Nude was a high point in an otherwise uneven auction, which totaled $491.4 million—above its $440 million low estimate but falling far short of the $705.8 million brought in by a similar sale earlier that year. While other records were set that night—including for works by Gustave Courbet, Balthus, and Roy Lichtenstein—the Modigliani painting stood out as the undeniable star of the evening, solidifying the artist’s status as one of the most sought-after names in the art market.

Sold for $179.4 million at Christie’s Latest York in May 2015.

In a recent development, pablo Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) (1955) set a upcoming auction record in 2015 when it sold for $179.4 million at Christie’s New York, becoming the most expensive painting ever sold at auction at the time. The painting, the final and most intricate piece in Picasso’s 15-work “Women of Algiers” series (1954–55), had an on-request estimate of around $140 million but soared past that figure after deep bidding.

The competition for the masterpiece played out entirely over the phone, with then-Christie’s executives Loic Gouzer and Brett Gorvy representing rival bidders. Pylkkänen, serving as auctioneer, declared “Still many people in the game” as bidding climbed past $140 million. Eventually, Gorvy’s bidder emerged victorious with a hammer price of $160 million, drawing cheers from the audience.

The “Women of Algiers” series was inspired by Eugène Delacroix’s 1834 masterpiece of the same name. Created in response to the Nationalist uprising in Algeria against French colonial rule, the series reflects Picasso’s fascination with both European Orientalist art and the evolving political landscape of the time. The version here is considered the most elaborate and fully realized of the set.

In a recent development, the painting had a notable provenance, originally acquired by Latest York collectors Victor and Sally Ganz directly from legendary dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler in 1956. It first appeared at auction in 1997, when it sold for $31.9 million—meaning its value increased nearly sixfold in less than two decades.

Recent findings suggest that while Christie’s maintained confidentiality regarding the winning bidder, reports later suggested that the buyer was former Qatari Prime Minister Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani. The sale reinforced Picasso’s dominance in the art market, cementing Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) as one of the defining auction moments of the decade.

Sold for $181.2 million at Christie’s New York in May 2026.

In a recent development, this 11-foot-wide painting by Jackson Pollock came to auction at Christie’s with both a first-class provenance and remarkable historical cachet. Pollock painted the work in 1948, the year after he first devised his drip painting technique, in which the artist flung his paint at the canvas rather than applying it directly using his brush. The technique distanced Pollock’s hand from his painting, leaving the application of his paint to chance.

Before he owned Sotheby’s, businessman A. Alfred Taubman owned the painting, selling it to publishing magnate S. I. Newhouse in 2000. In 2026, nearly a decade after Newhouse’s death, the painting headed to sale at Christie’s with a $100 million estimate, poising it to break Pollock’s record. At the time of the Christie’s auction, the painting hadn’t been seen publicly since 1977.

Recent findings suggest that the work ended up shooting far beyond its estimate and becoming one of the most expensive paintings ever sold. Bidding opened at $80 million, and following 60 bids, the painting hammered at $157 million. With fees, the total rose to $181.2 million.

On November 18, 2026, Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), a picture of sunlit trees set against oncoming storm clouds, sold for $190.4 million (including fees) at Sotheby’s. The cover lot for the auction house’s Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” it set a fresh auction record for the Dutch painter. The reported buyer was dealer William Acquavella.

The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold for $102 million. The latest result beat that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

That the sale happened at all was a victory for Sotheby’s. Just days before the auction, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement, clearing the painting’s title.

Industry observers note that painted shortly after Van Gogh arrived at Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Blossoming Chestnut Trees is among the 70-plus paintings (and more than 50 drawings) that the artist made there before taking his own life only two months later. It was also one of only eight Auvers landscapes still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

Recent findings suggest that the electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades. It was last exhibited at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in 1964 before Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro and Nelly Arrieta Blaquier, bought it in 1975—the kind of provenance and scarcity that fuels record-breaking prices like this one.—Daniel Cassady.

Sold for $195 million at Christie’s Upcoming York in May 2022.

According to recent reports, andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, one of the most iconic images in modern art, became the most expensive 20th-century artwork ever sold at auction when it fetched $195 million at Christie’s Latest York in 2022. The silkscreen portrait, based on a publicity still of Marilyn Monroe from the 1953 film Niagara, is part of Warhol’s famous “Shot Marilyn” series—named after a 1964 incident when performance artist Dorothy Podber fired a gun at a stack of Warhol’s canvases.

The work was the star lot of the evening, drawing competition from four bidders, including three on the phone and one in the room. Art dealer Larry Gagosian, bidding in person, ultimately secured the painting with a hammer price of $170 million, well below its $200 million estimate.

Industry observers note that the “Shot Marilyn” works are among Warhol’s most coveted pieces, with only five versions in existence. This particular portrait had been in a private collection for five decades, coming from the estate of Swiss dealers Thomas and Doris Ammann. With no financial guarantee, its sale marked a major moment for both the Warhol market and the broader contemporary art market.

In surpassing the $179.4 million record set by Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) (1955) in 2015, Shot Sage Blue Marilyn reaffirmed Warhol’s place at the pinnacle of modern art valuations. While some experts saw the sale as a watershed moment, others noted that privately brokered transactions for blue-chip artworks have long exceeded the $200 million mark.

In a recent development, gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16) became the second-most expensive artwork ever sold at auction when it achieved $236.4 million at Sotheby’s in November 2025, surpassing Klimt’s previous records and setting a new high for any work of modern art. The full-length portrait, one of only two named Klimt commissions in private hands, was the undisputed centerpiece of the sale of the Leonard A. Lauder Collection.

Sources indicate that bidding opened at $130 million and unfolded over 20 tense minutes, narrowing to two phone bidders represented by Sotheby’s specialists David Galperin and Julian Dawes. Dawes’s bidder ultimately won with a hammer price of $205 million, prompting applause in the salesroom and marking the most expensive lot ever handled by Sotheby’s. The result vaulted past Picasso’s Les Femmes d’Alger (Version ‘O’), which had held the record for a modern artwork at $179.4 million since 2015. Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, meanwhile, made global headlines when it skirted the $200 million mark in 2022.

The painting was commissioned by one of Klimt’s most important patron families, survived wartime confiscation, and was restituted in 1948 before entering Lauder’s collection in the 1980s. Estimated in excess of $150 million, it had been widely expected to challenge the artist’s previous high. Instead, it rewrote the record books—cementing Klimt as one of the few early-modern painters consistently capable of commanding nine-figure prices in today’s market, and potentially opening the door for even more masterpieces to break the $200 million barrier.

Sold for $450.3 million at Christie’s New York in November 2017.

In a landmark moment in the art world, Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi (c. 1500) set a latest record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction, fetching an astonishing $450.3 million at Christie’s in New York in November 2017. The sale, which took place in a packed salesroom at Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, was driven by an intense 19-minute bidding war.

Bidding began in earnest at $100 million—which was also the guarantee—and escalated rapidly from there, with cheers and applause breaking out as the painting crossed the $200 million threshold. Pylkkanen, again serving as auctioneer, skillfully kept the crowd engaged as bids climbed incrementally in the final moments. At one point, the bidding reached $350 million, before finally settling at $400 million, with an additional $50 million in fees for the buyer.

The Salvator Mundi’s journey to the auction block was filled with intrigue, including debates over its authenticity and a controversial restoration by conservator Dianne Modestini. Despite these uncertainties, the painting’s remarkable backstory and its connection to Leonardo da Vinci—whether authentic or not—captivated buyers. The work had once sold for just $1,175 in 2005, when it was attributed to a follower of Leonardo, but was later restored and re-attributed to the master himself.

Recent findings suggest that the sale marked a culmination of a carefully orchestrated marketing campaign by Christie’s, which included a global tour and celebrity endorsements, such as Patti Smith and Leonardo DiCaprio. The Salvator Mundi’s newly introduced auction price far eclipsed the previous record-holder, Pablo Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version O) (1955), which had sold for $179 million earlier that year.

This sale marked not only a record-breaking moment for the auction house but also highlighted the increasingly influential role of market value in the art world, where the price tag may overshadow the painting’s historical and artistic significance.

The buyer of Salvator Mundi was revealed a month after to the sale to be Saudi Arabian crown prince Mohammed Bin Salman, with quiet aims for it to eventually go on view in Riyadh.

#68669. Maren Hassinger Won’t Be Weighed Down

Maren Hassinger Won’t Be Weighed Down

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, maren Hassinger’s retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) has a radiant warmth about it—surprisingly so, given that it’s a show made mostly of gray metal sculptures whose edges could prick you raw.
  • Sources indicate that rejected in college from Bennington’s dance department in the 1960s, Hassinger was pushed toward sculpture by a teacher who noticed her gift.
  • In graduate school, at UCLA, Hassinger was rerouted once again after finding the sculpture program to be a boys’ club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, maren Hassinger’s retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) has a radiant warmth about it—surprisingly so, given that it’s a show made mostly of gray metal sculptures whose edges could prick you raw. This warmth owes a lot to the photographs, printed mural-sized and filling vitrines, taken by her long-term collaborator Adam Avila. Scattered throughout, they show Hassinger dancing, beaming, and/or hamming it up for the camera, often mirroring her sculpture’s forms with her body. But it owes, too, to the ways she rose to meet her career’s surprising twists and turns. Related Articles ARTnews Awards 2026 Lifetime Achievement: Maren Hassinger Maren Hassinger to Receive Her Largest Retrospective to Date Next Year.

Sources indicate that rejected in college from Bennington’s dance department in the 1960s, Hassinger was pushed toward sculpture by a teacher who noticed her gift. “My love of motion,” she states in the catalog, carried her from one to the other. Clement Greenberg was a guest at her senior thesis critique: He had “the gift of gab, but was a bit of a bully” she remembers with accurate alliterations. He would not be her last mean man.

In graduate school, at UCLA, Hassinger was rerouted once again after finding the sculpture program to be a boys’ club. As she remembers it, not one single woman was enrolled. So she found a home in fiber, a typical tale, and made it work: “Truthfully,” she admits in the catalog, “I was just trying to get a degree so I could teach and make art.” But she found herself too impatient for the loom and uninterested in making fabric. So she gathered fibers out in the world, chancing upon a weighty rope in a shipyard. It was made of blonde hemp but discolored by oil. Playing around, she eventually unraveled some of its strands before tying segments into a series of loose, giant macrame knots that greet visitors to BAMPFA, where they lie on the ground as if waiting to be pulled tight.

In a recent development, hassinger would marry craft techniques with industrial materials henceforth—a revealing portrait of women’s changing work in her time. She became such a regular at one LA wire shop that they featured her on the cover of their trade magazine. Soon, she was incorporating elevator cables—effectively wire ropes, their cords twisted together—into what would become her best known works. Leaning (1980) sees cables with frayed ends bundled in some two dozen bouquets. Only the central arrangement has a flat bottom and sits sturdily; the rest are free to lean.

Fiber meets metal in River, a 2,000-pound rope-chain Hassinger made as an ambitious graduate student in 1972. But where was a student to store such a behemoth? Recognition would not come until much later—as the title of her work Wallflower series (1975) attests—so she let River go, then finally remade it in 2011 for a Studio Museum acquisition. (Good thing she had so many photographs). A few other works at BAMPFA are recreations, too, but after school, she mainly made sculptures that could be coiled up and made compact: a resourceful response to the realities of real estate.

According to recent reports, to see Hassinger’s work is to think about the act of making it. It reveals you: Knots are blown up big so that you can see each twist and turn. Her titles are often verbs, as with Whirling (1978), Walking (1978), and Leaning (1980). “When she talks about the work, she moves” explained Margot Norton, who co-curated the show with Anthony Graham.

It has been revealed that hassinger met the obstacles that came her way, as a Black woman born in 1947, with poetry and practicality in equal measure. Of her turn to newspaper, which she twisted and knotted for a cascading 2008 installation, she explains that the material “is very handy and cheap [laughs].” But it also must have been cathartic to rip the headlines into strips. Her resourcefulness and resilience define the show, which sees her rethink sculpture without storage, fiber without fabric, choreography without corporeality.

Industry observers note that hassinger hardly did it alone. “Working alone is so antisocial” as she quips in the catalog. When Senga Nengudi first saw Hassinger’s work in 1975, she was thrilled to see another Black woman working with sculpture and performance, then looked her up. They became fast friends. With David Hammons, Nengudi then suggested that Linda Goode-Bryant show Hassinger at her gallery, Just Above Midtown (JAM). That show’s main work, Beach (1980), is installed at BAMPFA, too.

When Hassinger’s cohort of Black LA artists—known as Studio Z—lacked opportunities, they invented their own, as when Hassinger, Nengudi, Ulysses Jenkins, and others performed at the 1982 opening of “Afro-American Abstractions.” They had neither hung work on the walls nor been included in the checklist, but they did call up the Los Angeles Municipal Art Gallery to accept a nonexistent invitation: “We are so thrilled to be doing the opening performance!” they informed whoever answered the phone.

In the 1990s, Hassinger found herself without a studio. Starved for space, she turned to video. Birthright (2005) is nothing like her sculptures, but it will forever change how you see them. Onscreen, the artist interviews her uncle about her family tree. She learns that her grandmother, Puddin, had been the product both of incest and an interracial affair. Puddin’s parents hadn’t known that they were nephew and aunt, because Puddin’s father was born out of wedlock to his lover’s father who had a secret Native mistress.

Once the affair was discovered, Puddin was given away to a plantation caretaker who had been enslaved, and her father was lynched by a white mob. Puddin’s son—Hassinger’s dad—never talked about any of this: He was abandoned too by Puddin, then struggled to relate to women, cutting Hassinger out of the will and passing down patterns. “My legacy was to feel unloved,” the artist concludes in the video. But then the show keeps going.

Sources indicate that right next to Birthright, the curators installed Love (2008/2026), and it is here—halfway through the retrospective—that galleries of gray give way to hot pink. Plastic shopping bags filled with human breath and love notes cover the walls. Her lightness beams off the building, but look closely and you’ll find a sense of play throughout the show.

Thinking about familial lineages, Hassinger’s knots and ropes start to feel like umbilical cords severed and frayed. History is hefty, but it never weighs the work down in any sense of the word. “I always felt so good when I danced,” the artist explains, “lighter, faster.” It is easy to imagine her dancing in her studio while walking around BAMPFA, where one gets a sense of heaviness made to look light. Untitled (1972/2020) sees ropes with looped ends, noose-like, but instead of being tied into knots, strands are undone and then woven back together seamlessly. In the galleries, the ropes dangle gracefully from the ceiling and weigh heavy on the floor.

Hassinger is an artist who sees things soberly as they are and imaginatively as they might be—a gift that enables her to turn junkyard findings into elegant arrays and litter into love.

Why has North Korea redesigned its flag? It's not about aesthetics...

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite being a failed nation in most regards (60% are thought to be below the poverty line, and reports of widespread starvation have surfaced as recently as 2021), North Korea continues to fascinate us.
  • As the summit wrapped up today, though, Kim Jong Un was nowhere to be seen.
  • Well, earlier this month it emerged that the highly secretive and repressive nation has changed the shape of its flag for the first time since 1948.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite being a failed nation in most regards (60% are thought to be below the poverty line, and reports of widespread starvation have surfaced as recently as 2021), North Korea continues to fascinate us. Even this week, as Trump, Putin and Xi prepared to meet in Shenzhen, China the media was playing "Where's Kim?" after Trump told reporters North Korean leader Kim Jong Un "would like to" attend, and that whether he came was "up to President Xi".

As the summit wrapped up today, though, Kim Jong Un was nowhere to be seen. Instead, state media revealed him touring a half-built ski resort at home. Which is shame for a design obsessive like me. Because if he had turned up, I'd have been watching the flagpoles rather than the handshakes.

Sources indicate that why? Well, earlier this month it emerged that the highly secretive and repressive nation has changed the shape of its flag for the first time since 1948.

It has been revealed that the revised constitution, ratified in March but only recently published on the state website, sets the ratio at 1:1.65 rather than the old 1:2. The white stripes look noticeably thicker, and the red star in its white circle now sits closer to the centre. The government, though hasn't explained why, so it's up to us to have an educated guess.

It has been revealed that it's tempting to read this in pure design terms, as a long overdue tidy-up. Indeed, as long ago as 1948, one delegate worried the long, thin flag would fold too easily on the pole. And things do move slowly in state bureaucracies, after all. Not usually this slowly, but could it just be that sorting out the flag's ratio has finally just floated to the top of a long list of priorities?

If it were as simple as that, though, North Korea would presumably have gone for the standard ratio of 2:3, the one seen in over 80 national flags. France, Spain, Italy, Netherlands, China, Russia, Ukraine… you get the picture. Instead Pyongyang has opted for on 1:1.65, a ratio seen in… absolutely no other national flag on Earth. Which kind of suggests they're trying to make a point.

It has been revealed that the professed meaning behind the design has shifted too. The white elements once stood for the purity of a single Korean people. Naenara now indicates they represent the loyalty of people who support the Party and the leader.

You might think "so what?", but this actually a very big deal. Ever since North and South Korea were split between the communist and capitalist powers in 1945, both sides have dreamed the unification of the country (albeit under their control, of course).

In 2023, though, Kim expounded the "two hostile states" doctrine, which mentioned that reunification “can never be achieved” with South Korea. In 2024 he rewrote the national anthem along these lines, and the new flag design should be seen in the same light.

It's a bit like when you give up on getting back with an ex-partner: you go out and buy a whole latest outfit to cheer yourself up and show them you're doing just fine without them.

Industry observers note that so while the flag design that has barely changed, that's doesn't mean it's not significant. The fact that it's changed at all actually states a lot about the future of 70 million Koreans, and the global world order as a whole.

#68667. Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (895 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation.
  • The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected.
  • It has been revealed that “These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

It has been revealed that “These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

Industry observers note that the research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

The researchers discovered that while participants mentioned they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

In a recent development, “We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”.

Ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh says. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”.

People are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher states she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”.

It has been revealed that these chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

According to recent reports, “Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen claims. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a significant impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen claims.

Sources indicate that over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan indicates. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Sources indicate that of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan indicates. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”.

It has been revealed that ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she states. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”.

#68666. Ireland’s Experiment in Paying Artists a Basic Income Is Working as Intended For Artists

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1173 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Artnews ↗ Open Full Page

Ireland’s Experiment in Paying Artists a Basic Income Is Working as Intended For Artists

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Life was pretty rosy for the 2,000 Irish artists who landed a spot on Ireland’s Basic Income for the Arts (BIA) pilot scheme.
  • In a recent development, now in its fourth year, DGW was launched in 2023 by the city’s commercial galleries to raise the profile of its contemporary art scene.
  • According to recent reports, while the artists I spoke to described the BIA as a major boost to their working lives, I found little evidence that it has fundamentally changed Dublin’s contemporary art scene.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Life was pretty rosy for the 2,000 Irish artists who landed a spot on Ireland’s Basic Income for the Arts (BIA) pilot scheme. For three years, from 2022 to 2025, €325 arrived in their bank accounts every week. The money was intended to provide a dependable income, reduce the need to take on unrelated jobs to cover living costs, and give artists more time to concentrate on making art. Judging by the recipients I spoke earlier this month at Dublin Gallery Weekend (DGW), the pilot was a success. And since the BIA was made permanent in February, thousands more artists are hoping to reap the rewards.“Basic Income for the Arts is a game changer, and now it is here to stay,” Ireland’s minister for culture, communications, and sport, Patrick O’Donovan, said in February. Related Articles Ireland's Museum Staffers Struggle with Precarious Contracts and Toxic Environments National Museum of Ireland Employee Charged in Alleged Car Bomb Plot.

In a recent development, now in its fourth year, DGW was launched in 2023 by the city’s commercial galleries to raise the profile of its contemporary art scene. Organized by the Contemporary Art Gallery Association (CAGA), this year’s four-day program brought together galleries and cultural institutions for exhibitions, talks, screenings, and performances. A major addition was the inaugural Francis Bacon Awards for Irish Visual Arts, a €40,000 prize fund supported by Château La Coste. Painter Patrick Graham received the €25,000 Lifetime Achievement Award, while Belfast-born artist Cathy Wilkes took the €15,000 Mid-Career prize. Both will stage solo exhibitions at Château La Coste in Provence, France.

According to recent reports, while the artists I spoke to described the BIA as a major boost to their working lives, I found little evidence that it has fundamentally changed Dublin’s contemporary art scene. None of the dealers, curators, or museum directors I spoke to suggested that its impact had been felt on a wider scale across the city’s galleries or commercial market.

According to recent reports, applications for the BIA’s upcoming three-year round opened in May, with previous recipients eligible to reapply for one of the 2,000 available places. Around 10,000 artists applied, making competition fierce for a program to which the Irish government has committed €18 million.

In a recent development, “Over the course of the scheme, my practice flourished,” Dublin-based artist Gearóid O’Dea, who was selected for the pilot, told ARTnews. The funding allowed him to curate an exhibition based on Samuel Beckett’s work that travelled to Berlin, and collaborate with four other artists through the Glue Factory collective. He said the financial support made it possible to bring artists together and exhibit internationally without constantly having to find other jobs to make ends meet.

In a recent development, cork-born Elinor O’Donovan, who is now studying for a master’s degree in Gothenburg, Sweden, also received the pilot payment. She told ARTnews that “it completely transformed my ability to work as an artist.”.

Before joining the scheme, O’Donovan worked part-time as a receptionist alongside her artistic practice. The weekly payment allowed her to give up the job and concentrate on making art full-time. “Knowing the money was coming for three years was a big relief,” she noted. “My psychological wellbeing improved because there was security.”.

It has been revealed that lauren, another former recipient who is now based in London, stated the payment arrived at a pivotal moment in her career. Having just completed her undergraduate degree, she had secured a graduate residency at the Royal Hibernian Academy in Dublin, where she was given a studio and access to painting classes. The BIA helped her develop her practice and take up further opportunities, including residencies and exhibitions. She has since secured funding to continue her studies in London. “There’s kind of nothing I haven’t done in the last four or five years that hasn’t, in some way, been impacted by my experience with the basic income,” she told ARTnews.

Despite the BIA’s unprecedented support for artists, not everyone is waxing lyrical about it, including some who benefited from the original pilot. Tadhg Ó Cuirrín, a visual artist who received the payment and works with the artists’ trade union Praxis, believes the government has missed an opportunity to build on its success. More than 10,000 artists applied for the upcoming round, yet the number of places remains unchanged at 2,000. Recipients will also be limited to three years of support in every six-year period.

“It feels less like a base income per se and more like a kind of a multi-annual grant chosen by lottery,” he told ARTnews.

Sources indicate that although the program is now permanent, individual artists are not guaranteed support beyond three years. Artists must meet the scheme’s eligibility criteria, after which places are allocated through a lottery, with selection also taking demographic representation into account. Ó Cuirrín argued that the three-years-on, three-years-off model reinstates the financial insecurity BIA was designed to address. Artists risk losing their income just as their practices are beginning to flourish.

Sources indicate that O’Dea has reapplied for the new round but is still waiting to hear if he’s been selected. He remarked the prospect of losing the regular income has brought financial anxiety back into his life.

It has been revealed that the transition has also caused difficulties for artists who relied on other forms of state support. Michaële Cutaya, a spokesperson for Praxis, previously told The Art Newspaper that some former recipients have had to return to other work to cover their living costs. “If you have to then take on a different kind of job, it’s really disruptive,” she noted.

Noel Kelly, chief executive of Visual Artists Ireland, remarked he welcomes the permanent scheme, but pointed to practical problems. BIA payments can affect artists receiving means-tested benefits, including disability allowance, while some applicants’ immigration status may prevent them from registering as self-employed, a requirement for participation.

Kelly also cautioned against judging the program solely on its financial return. An independent evaluation estimated that every euro invested generated €1.39 in social and economic benefits, taking into account factors including improved wellbeing. Kelly remarked that calculation misses much of what artists contribute to society.

Sources indicate that “I hate that argument,” he told ARTnews. “It allows us to participate one in the local community, two in the local economy, three in the local creative ecology.”.

The impact of the BIA on Ireland’s commercial art market is harder to measure. John Daly, director of Hillsboro Fine Art and chair of the Contemporary Art Gallery Association, told ARTnews that the country’s galleries continue to operate with a relatively small pool of collectors. “Success actually is survival,” he said. Daly argued the Irish art scene needs to attract younger collectors and encourage greater corporate support. Despite the presence of major international technology companies like Google in Dublin, he said corporate collecting remains limited, with companies tending to support arts initiatives such as murals and workshops. “It should be a huge opportunity, given the presence of all these multinationals, but not yet.”.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

How to pick the right website template for your creative business

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that even if you're using one of the best website builders, I recommend taking your time when choosing your template if you're going that route.
  • According to recent reports, templates can still offer substantial value by handling the heavy lifting of page structure, navigation, and responsive design.
  • In this guide, we'll cover the key factors to consider when evaluating templates, and also what other options are available if a template-based approach isn't the best match for your project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that even if you're using one of the best website builders, I recommend taking your time when choosing your template if you're going that route. A website template provides the foundation for everything, and choosing wisely at the beginning can save you time and energy further down the line.

According to recent reports, templates can still offer substantial value by handling the heavy lifting of page structure, navigation, and responsive design. But with countless websites vying for attention, you'll want a starting point that aligns with your brand while leaving plenty of scope for customisation so you can make the site stand out and add features or adapt the site later without requiring a complete overhaul.

In this guide, we'll cover the key factors to consider when evaluating templates, and also what other options are available if a template-based approach isn't the best match for your project.

Recent findings suggest that modern templates aren't intended to be finished websites but to provide a flexible framework that can be reshaped to fit your needs. That noted, it's still important to check that a template includes all the layout and navigation features you think you're going to need. Success comes down to choosing a template that's already close to your brand's requirements, then refining and personalising it until the final result feels unique and tailored rather than generic.

According to recent reports, pay close attention to the underlying framework, including page layout, content hierarchy and overall site structure. Modern website builders make it relatively simple to enhancement colors, typography, images and other visual details, but altering navigation systems, restructuring pages, or reworking the flow of content can be far more time-consuming, so these are areas to check.

According to recent reports, make sure the template offers the sections or content blocks that you need. This might include a hero image, features, testimonials and galleries. You might only want a simple one pager, but remember that it's easier to simplify a complex template than it is to add structure to one that's overly basic. Templates that provide little flexibility could limit future content growth.

Sources indicate that check the menu organisation fits with the structure you want before committing. Look for a clear visual hierarchy that guides visitors to important content, intuitive menus that make sections easy to find, flexible page layouts that support your content requirements and logical placements for calls to action, such as contact forms or portfolio links.

According to recent reports, avoid choosing a template based solely on appearance without considering usability or selecting complex navigation structures that confuse visitors. Overcrowded layouts can confuse viewers with elements that compete for attention.

The visual style of a template should complement your brand rather than dominate it, and design elements should align with your brand identity and audience expectations.

Recent findings suggest that most modern templates will allow considerable customisation, so you don't necessarily need one that resembles your branding from the start, but it can save time. Even then, publishing a template without significant customisation is rarely enough so check that typography and spacing can be easily adapted and that the colour palette can be customised. Also check that visual styling is consistent throughout the template.

Web design trends come and go. In 2026, we're seeing a lot of glassmorphism, immersive 3D visuals and storytelling through motion. But avoid picking a trendy design that may date quickly. Using a template with excessive animations or visual effects can also cause a site to date, while also potentially impacting on loading times and user engagement.

With visitors browsing on desktops, tablets and smartphones, responsive design is essential. Check how the template adapts across devices, as restructuring mobile layouts requires advanced customisation.

Sources indicate that that means more than just checking that the layout adapts to the different screen size and orientation. Also evaluate whether animations, transitions, and interactive components work across platforms and match your brand's personality.

Recent findings suggest that while most templates today are responsive, don't assume completely responsive behaviour without testing it. Look for layouts that adapt smoothly to different screen sizes, readable text and appropriately sized buttons on mobile devices and fast-loading pages across platforms. Functionality should ideally be consistent regardless of device.

Recent findings suggest that prioritising responsiveness can also mean avoiding designs that rely heavily on large images or complex interactions. Make sure you remember to check how portfolios, galleries or forms display on smaller screens.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA.

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new consumers: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Breaking: Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity.
  • Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.
  • At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

According to recent reports, “Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

According to recent reports, they also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik says.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

Running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

Incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik says. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”.

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

“Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik claims. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

Sources indicate that the steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”.

Still, it’s notable to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she says.

In fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik indicates.

In a recent development, both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

If you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik claims. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

But if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik says.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Industry observers note that beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s important to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

Industry observers note that “Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik claims. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”.

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

Ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.

  • Having spent time in Leonida myself for my GTA 6 review, often just people-watching, eavesdropping on conversations, and spying on the game's background actors as they play out their lives, I can say this is the most alive game I've played.
  • With all I've seen, I can see why Rockstar's art team is so keen to talk about its pedestrians and background characters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every open-world game has a crowd problem. Pack the streets with people and, sooner or later, you clock the same jogger for the fifth time, and the illusion falls apart. GTA 6 breaks that wall and delivers a world filled with unique little virtual actors.

Having spent time in Leonida myself for my GTA 6 review, often just people-watching, eavesdropping on conversations, and spying on the game's background actors as they play out their lives, I can say this is the most alive game I've played. A regular couple rant about gentrification and other conspiracies on their apartment steps; two others argue about that latest Manatees result; two women sip coffee, gossiping about their friend's love life; one's eyes widen, brows lift, just a fraction too slowly to feel like shock.

With all I've seen, I can see why Rockstar's art team is so keen to talk about its pedestrians and background characters.

Valmor Garcia, Senior Technical Art Director: Dynamic Art, says Rockstar has moved on from the “monolithic” NPCs of GTAV and Red Dead Redemption 2, which were built to lower visual standards than those of the games’ main casts. The aim now is “fully fleshed-out characters with singular awareness and visual identities”, driven by dynamic moods and personalities, with their own anatomy, facial features and dialogue.

Sources indicate that garcia puts all of that on a visual par with Jason and Lucia. He also says it’s the first time Rockstar feels it has levelled the whole cast so consistently, including world NPCs.

In a recent development, valmor Garcia, Senior Technical Art Director: Dynamic Art, states Rockstar has moved on from the “monolithic” NPCs of GTAV and Red Dead Redemption 2, which were built to lower visual standards than those of the games’ main casts. The aim now is “fully fleshed-out characters with singular awareness and visual identities”, driven by dynamic moods and personalities, with their own anatomy, facial features and dialogue.

According to recent reports, garcia puts all of that on a visual par with Jason and Lucia. He also notes it’s the first time Rockstar feels it has levelled the whole cast so consistently, including world NPCs.

Mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, conveys the scale. “There are close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities,” he states, “then we layer in hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences to punctuate the world and reward exploration.”.

Those everyday sets, with people hanging out and doing day-to-day jobs, “form the foundation of this living world”, according to Tennant. The variety extends to bodies, too. The team decided early to “really push the variation in character sizes and body types”, which meant building “a very robust way to share animations between characters”.

Garcia says the team built new technology and tools “from the ground up” for the engine. The all-new in-house tech covers hair, cloth simulation and head-and-body customisation, and it’s applied across the world “to benefit all characters equally”. So the people on the street get the same tech as the leads.

It’s the little things that sell it. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, says that “everywhere you look, little stories constantly unfold”. That might be as simple as what someone’s wearing, how they walk and talk, or what they’re blasting from a passing car.

I see this in how characters dress and behave differently across the map. Some things are just obvious, such as characters wearing swimsuits on the beach, but Rockstar takes it further, as Leonida's beachgoers lie and chat on towels, play frisbee, and make mistakes – I snuck onto a boat party and watched as characters danced and reacted to Lucia and Jason's moves.

In a recent development, most of the people you pass in Leonida will only be on screen for a moment, but Rockstar has built them as if you might stop and look; in fact, the developer wants you to stop, look and listen, and simply love being in the world. Sam Fender's People Watching is on the soundtrack for a reason.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines.
