  • I have just seen Michael (the fresh Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release.
  • On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

I have just seen Michael (the fresh Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She says almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

In person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

In a recent development, “There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she says. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s important to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”.

Recent findings suggest that long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

In a recent development, “My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she says. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”.

In a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”.

Long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

It has been revealed that “The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I said money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”.

In a recent development, once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”.

According to recent reports, now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft newly introduced stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

“This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”.

In talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

“Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

"You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

In a recent development, she laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

In a recent development, in 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

“The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”.

According to recent reports, that clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

“I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is big. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She indicates all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

Recent findings suggest that in the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she states. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”.

I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

Long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

“I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”.

The memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

“In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she says. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother mentioned it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”.

That an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a new idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

“Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

Sources indicate that but Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole fresh body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

“I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she notes. “I find the balance.”.

Beauty was never her primary currency, she notes. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

Our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

Sources indicate that “Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she notes. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the substantial stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”.

In a recent development, the Siza Award is an annual architecture prize established by the Serralves Foundation to honor socially responsible design and public architecture. It places special emphasis on architectural generosity and targets emerging practices and architects in their thirties and forties with demonstrated sensitivity to local communities, territory, and the environment. The recognition is grounded in the conviction, reflected in Siza's career, that architects are agents of change with the ability to influence democratic discourse, whether in rebuilding urban identities or promoting social inclusion. As stated by the Foundation, the new generation of architects it targets now faces the challenge "to bridge the gap between human scarcity and technological advancement, rethinking the rules of the game and exploring archetypes, materials, shelters, labor, and other ways of improving life as a whole.".

#68589. How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1478 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting.
  • Sources indicate that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships.
  • Going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting. For a while, that little phrase has been used to describe the experience of executing the bare minimum at work without actually leaving your job: You do just enough to get by but never rise above that benchmark to prove yourself or exceed expectations. It’s a strategy that can keep you employed while preserving your mental and emotional energy.

Sources indicate that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships. And, yes, it could also apply to the one you have with your mom. Though you’re probably not collecting paychecks here, maintaining a relationship with your mother may connect you to crucial resources you need to get by. Maybe your mom really does play a big role in your finances, or she’s your source of health insurance. She could also be a connection to your culture or other family members that you don’t want to distance yourself from. Logistics aside, you might just want some distance from your mom without sacrificing your emotional connection. As I learned from reporting my book Motherf*cked: How to Keep Your Mother’s Toxic Drama From Ruining Your Life, those are all solid reasons to maintain a relationship that leaves you exhausted.

Going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact. However, there’s no official definition, therapist Whitney Goodman, LMFT, told me in an interview for Motherf*cked. For some, it could look like avoiding one-on-one visits but checking in via text, email, quarterly phone calls, or greeting cards. Or you could catch up in person while avoiding the details of your life. The frequency of low-contact contact varies too. Some would say talking once a week is low-contact for them. Others might say once a year.

Recent findings suggest that the reasons why people go low-contact differ as much as the ways it can look. Generally speaking, taking space can be useful anytime a relationship feels painful or draining. It gives you more time, energy, and emotional bandwidth to take care of yourself and tend to other important parts of your life.

Recent findings suggest that that can be especially helpful in our relationships with our moms, a dynamic that, for many reasons, is often packed with emotional triggers. If spending time with your mom feels exhausting, you’re sick of always stressing about this relationship, or you’ve tried and failed to set boundaries with her in the past, pulling back might be helpful here, Goodman says. If you can relate, here’s how to do that.

Ideally, this process is a series of experiments where you pull back from the relationship in different ways to see what feels good and what doesn’t, Goodman explains. You can then use that information to determine how much contact is too much—or not enough. Here’s how to get started.

Industry observers note that going low-contact is really just setting a boundary, or defining what behavior you will or won’t tolerate. You’re showing others how you want to be treated. Sometimes, people don’t like being restricted and get messy when limits are put on their relationships. Moms can be like that too.

If you’ve already tried to set boundaries with your mom by, say, not answering every one of her calls or telling her that you don’t want to talk about your dating life, now is a good time to reflect on how that went.

In a recent development, moms who are receptive to those guardrails may be easygoing about any additional boundaries. That could mean you don’t need to cut as many points of contact to feel better about the relationship. On the other hand, if your mom has blown through your boundaries in the past, you might need stronger limitations to protect your peace today. Keep that in mind for the next step.

Again, there is no official criterion defining a low-contact relationship, so don’t get hung up on labels. First, think about how much contact you have now. How often do you spend time together? What does that time look like? What would you change to make this relationship less taxing?

Maybe you see your mom every Sunday, let her come over unannounced, and answer all of her texts—even the ones you’d rather not. Consider which of these interactions take the most out of you, and ask yourself, Would eliminating this point of contact make the relationship less exhausting overall?

You could start small by taking a beat to check in with yourself before responding to your mom’s texts. If you don’t feel like dealing with her at that moment, don’t. If that’s not enough to preserve your energy, maybe you can limit the number of texts you’ll respond to each day or week. You can always change it up later by removing another point of contact, like those unannounced visits, if you need more space (see step five).

You don’t have to formally announce that you’re going low-contact, but giving your mom a heads-up might be useful.

Industry observers note that if you’re not worried about your safety and your quiet quitting tactics mean your mom has to change her behavior, then laying out your plans could make sense. Plus, explaining why you put them in place might help you resolve whatever is behind your decision to quiet quit this relationship.

That remarked, if your version of low-contact doesn’t require anything from your mom, you don’t need to tell her it’s happening, says Goodman. For example, you can hold back information about your life or avoid certain events without discussing it first.

In a recent development, feel weird about this? I get that, but here’s something to think about: You’ve probably told your mom about the ways she’s hurt you many, many times before, notes Goodman. Even if you haven’t explicitly pointed to every single occasion she hurt your feelings, your body language and tone of voice likely have conveyed how her actions impacted you. You may be tired of retelling those painful events, which is why you’d like to avoid another confrontation with your mom. So consider this your permission not to.

According to recent reports, still, your mom might notice you pulling back and ask what’s going on. If she does, you can tell her why you’re not getting into your dating life or attending the family reunion. You don’t have to, though. You’re welcome to make excuses or just say, “Yep, you’re right, I’m not doing that anymore.” You don’t owe her an explanation.

Goodman claims the best way to tell how going low-contact is working for you is to check in with your emotions as much as possible. You can write them down in your journal, use a mood- or emotions-tracking app, or bring them up to your therapist.

It has been revealed that yes, the feelings you’re tracking can be related to your mom and quiet quitting her, but don’t forget about all the others, says Goodman. It might not be obvious which feelings are related to your maternal figure and which aren’t. After breaking patterns that existed for a long time, you might get a sense that something is off. Maybe you feel purposeless or lost. Maybe it’s like you forgot something on your way to the airport, but you don’t know what it is.

Recent findings suggest that all of that is normal, indicates Goodman. So is feeling like you really miss your mom, even if you know you did the right thing. Of course, everyone’s situation is different. Maybe you don’t truly miss her, but miss the idea of a person she’ll never be. When quiet quitting is working, those feelings should come up less frequently and/or become less intense. At the same time, you’ll likely feel some relief. You could notice more peace in your life and more space to focus on things other than your mom.

You can always tweak how much contact you have with your mom. Ideally, this involves a continuous assessment of what’s working and what’s not. If the low-contact strategy you’ve established feels sustainable and makes you less obsessive or overwhelmed by the relationship—and your mom is able to abide by your rules—you might have found a solution. Success!

Industry observers note that if this version of quiet quitting doesn’t keep your mom from violating your boundaries, emotionally manipulating you, or still leaves you drained, anxious, or depressed, you could level up, indicates Goodman. That means starting back at step one and quitting other parts of your relationship until you reach a point that feels sustainable.

In a recent development, remember, the goal is for you to feel less stressed about your interactions with your mom. By finding a routine that works for you, you can protect the parts of your relationship that you love and lose the rest.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.

Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.

Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.

Framery aims to tackle this glitch with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.

It has been revealed that “The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” said Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”.

“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.

For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.

The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.

“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”.

Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.

“Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” stated Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”.

As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

It has been revealed that according to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.

During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-new condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.

“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”.

To learn more, visit Framery’s website.

That fateful stab in your side is most likely to happen during exercise where your upper bod claims tight and upright for an extended period, such as when you run, jog, bike, hike, play soccer, etc.

Experts also theorize that it could be triggered by the boost of blood flow around the diaphragm when running.

Furthermore, fueling up before a big race is excellent — but eating or drinking large quantities right before running may boost your risk of getting a side stitch, anecdotal reports suggest.

Here, we look at project ideas in the United Kingdom, China, Cyprus, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Canada. They include a 10-bedroom wellness retreat in Kent; a community health service center in Tengjiao; a day center in Nicosia designed as a sensory-regulation system for adults on the severe end of the autism spectrum; and a daycare and rehabilitation facility in Antakya. Three hospital proposals in Khobar, Mississauga and London address teaching missions, digital connectivity and the phased replacement of existing facilities, showing how the idea of care is approached across very different scales.

Sources indicate that picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Recent findings suggest that here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so proposal accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

Another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s fresh function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts noted.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”.

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be confirmed on 26 November.

Recent findings suggest that comprising three reuse projects, RIAS noted this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “notable conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

We checked in with a doctor to find out.

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” claims Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov indicates.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”.

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:.

Vukasinov notes that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:.

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s vital to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

According to recent reports, remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a big hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, MAJOR designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.
  • Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture studio MASSIVE has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, MAJOR designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.

Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s newly introduced Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,.

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a fresh development,” MASSIVE partner Sören Grünert noted.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”.

It has been revealed that the hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

Here, projecting bays and set-back terraces will help to create privacy for the residents, whose homes will overlook a shared courtyard.

MAJOR used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

BIG also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

The first monograph devoted to the built work of Alejandro Muñoz Miranda (Granada, 1974), architect and professor of Architectural Design at the School of Architecture of Granada. The book brings together twelve works completed between 2004 and 2026 which, across very different programmes, keep returning to the same concerns: geometry, light and tectonics, the line of thought the author developed in his doctoral thesis with Kenneth Frampton.

In a recent development, the journey begins with institutional headquarters in Granada —the Confederation of Employers of Granada and the UGT and CC.OO. trade union buildings—, continues with the Children's Centre in El Chaparral, Albolote, and the urban scale of the remodelling of Gran Vía de Colón and the Avenida de la Constitución boulevard, and moves on to the funeral parlour in Murtas and two private houses, Agüera and Almagro. Collective housing fills the final section: the rental housing building in Málaga, winner of the Andalusia Architecture Award 2024, the 66 homes with terraces in Estepona and the Alborada residential building in Granada. The book closes with a small hotel at the foot of the Alhambra.

#68571. Tech Report: Surrogacy Nearly Destroyed Our Marriage. It Also Brought Us Back

📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1782 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Surrogacy Nearly Destroyed Our Marriage. It Also Brought Us Back

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.
  • After our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew.
  • It felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.

After our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew. I wasn’t so sure. For months, it had felt like my husband Ethan and I were two bodies fumbling to find each other in the dark. At home, our orbits rarely intersected. My eyes barely landed on Ethan. Once, he didn’t realize I was right behind him and he closed the door on me.

It felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble. We weathered life-altering challenges together in our 20s and 30s due to my whole-body symptoms from endometriosis, adenomyosis, early menopause, and a medical system that trivialized them all. My condition rattled our intimacy, upended my career, and made Ethan my caretaker. Being undiagnosed for decades also cost us my fertility, depleting my ovarian reserve and leading to miscarriage after miscarriage with IVF and IUIs.

Though we weren’t living the life we dreamed, and I felt guilty for the weight I foisted on Ethan, we managed to maintain the joie de vivre we’d had since we first met—until we turned to surrogacy.

Industry observers note that our decision to opt for an egg donor and a surrogate was an act of compromise. Though I’d always been ambivalent about motherhood, the idea of coparenting with Ethan had gradually filled me with tenderness and curiosity. But by then, after years of illness, I wanted a hysterectomy. Ethan still really wanted to be a dad. Neither of us wanted to jeopardize my wellness with more hormonal treatments and pregnancy losses, so we took what people called the “easy way out.” Though I was criticized by my doctors for giving up on my eggs and my uterus “too soon,” our decision to pursue surrogacy felt liberating—at first.

Sources indicate that we thought finding a gestational surrogate would be the hardest part. Turns out, we were wrong. Instead, we were totally unprepared for the ways surrogacy was going to change our marriage.

Our first surrogacy experience was the kind we now caution other intended parents against. We entrusted an agency with our fate and our funds, putting them in charge of introducing us to a surrogate and acting as the intermediary who would reimburse her for pregnancy-related expenses on our behalf. At the time, we were unaware of their proven fraudulent history.

Industry observers note that not only were Ethan and I new to surrogacy, but we also felt vulnerable—maybe even desperate. We were privileged to have found someone who wanted to do this for us, and we wanted to be generous and grateful. You also don’t have much control when your baby is in someone else’s womb and your funds are in a corporation’s bank account. So we ignored the red flags we noticed with the agency’s inflated reimbursements and our surrogate’s jarring mood fluctuations.

If we’d shared our worries with each other early on, we may have had a chance to course-correct. At least I wouldn’t have felt so alone carrying this angst in my bones. At one of our second-trimester ultrasounds, I resented Ethan for being his jovial self while he talked to our active baby boy through the screen as I stood hunched against the wall, struggling to feel present. It wasn’t just that the pregnancy felt unbearably abstract for me as a mother who didn’t contribute her genes or her womb; I was also increasingly skeptical of the agency and walking on eggshells with our surrogate, who’d keep us at arm’s length one week and accuse us of not being supportive enough the next. I’d never gotten this far in a pregnancy and it should have been a happy time. Instead, I bottled up my distress and couldn’t breathe from the weight of it.

It has been revealed that during our first surrogacy experience, Ethan let me bear the brunt of the conversations with our surrogate. He thought he had a supportive role, but his not being in the foreground put extra weight on my shoulders and took my time, energy, and headspace while sparing him. I was also the one who handled all the legal and financial paperwork, and the communication with the agency. Ethan was grateful and proud of me for managing what he considered more in my wheelhouse than his, but I felt paralyzing stress and resentment having to tackle these hard tasks on my own at such a vulnerable time.

In a recent development, our breaking point was brought on by our different ways of grieving. While I naturally tend to dig deep into painful topics and emotions to make sense of them, Ethan prefers to compartmentalize. At the hospital after the delivery, Ethan preferred to leave the room when I stayed to spend a few minutes with our stillborn. I wanted the loss to feel more tangible, while he wanted to hold onto the joy from other memories, like when we saw him on ultrasounds. Neither of us was wrong, but we were disconnected.

Recent findings suggest that the months that followed were agony because none of the doctors would counsel us on why our baby had died simply because I wasn’t the pregnant patient, as though we weren’t his parents and didn’t have the right to know. I spiraled into depression and was furious every time Ethan would tell his parents that we were fine. He didn’t want to burden them, but I didn’t want to mask our reality for the sake of others’ comfort. For 24 years—through long distance, sickness, and grief—we’d been the “strong couple” who never argued. Now, in the complexity of surrogacy, we kept snapping at each other because Ethan needed a semblance of normalcy and I needed to dwell in darkness.

In a recent development, so how do you come back to each other when who you were didn’t survive? Over nearly a year, thanks to our self-awareness, deep respect for one another, and therapy (which Ethan hated attending but did when required), we made three tiny shifts that saved our marriage.

Sources indicate that when we met our second surrogate through a more ethical, transparent, and supportive agency that did not demand funds in trust, Ethan and I formed a true trio with her. It helped that she considered us a team and wanted our involvement in appointments, decisions, and her daily life. She’d use the word “together” so often that it initially triggered us; it felt so foreign to us after our first surrogacy journey, and we couldn’t tell which of the two experiences was the anomaly. Ethan made it a priority to participate in our conversations and replied to our group texts if I couldn’t. We all shared freely—our fears, dreams, victories, recipes, and silly inside jokes—and the three of us built an intimacy I never expected. When it was just the two of us, our surrogate was never far from our thoughts, as if our marriage had expanded to include her.

In a recent development, ethan also started to help me with the challenging legal and financial tasks. He kept up with emails he was CC’ed on during the day and sat with me if we had paperwork to tackle, his hand on my back if I got overwhelmed.

Recent findings suggest that when we lost our baby with our second surrogate at the end of the first trimester, we grieved as a unit. Our trio sat intertwined, our hands piled on my lap. At home, Ethan was more receptive to my needs on my bad days. Just watching him witness me in those moments, even if all he did was listen and sigh, brought us closer together. I was more understanding when he clung to his social activities to blow off steam. Ethan was more honest with family and friends about our emotional and financial distress. He agreed to ask for help and for a loan to help us get back on our feet after two surrogacy journeys and thirteen years of fertility and ongoing health expenses.

Industry observers note that we decided not to talk about surrogacy on weekends or right before bed to give our nervous systems a chance to unwind. Dark humor helped us grieve: We’d sometimes whisper jaded comments to each other when triggered. When we imagine something creative we would have done with our kid, we say, “File it under never!” During the holidays, Ethan toasted me with, “Cheers to not losing a child this Christmas!” Holding space for our contrasting ways of grieving and meeting in the middle helped dissolve the resentment and tension between us.

According to recent reports, fertility treatments and surrogacy can become all-consuming for a couple, especially after decades of illness and loss. Being diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after our first surrogacy experience further shook my identity. We started making a conscious effort to remember what was special about our life and our love before all this. We are more than what we carry and what we’ve lost.

Besides carving out periods of play, nature, and grief-free talk, we also pushed ourselves to keep money aside for leisure and travel—not just for our living expenses and surrogacy costs—so we can look forward to something in our calendar and savor new experiences together.

In a recent development, we found, though, that the least daunting way of rebuilding our future is to simply take care of our present. Often, all we can handle is the next half-hour: where to take a walk, what to make for supper, how to support each other right then. I worked hard to keep my eyes focused on Ethan until it became natural again. Even now, as we grapple with whether and how to continue with our surrogacy journey, when we start acting like passing ships because of our full heads and aching hearts, we drop everything, hug, touch.

I never expected our strong marriage to be impacted by the most tender gift we gave each other: the chance to grow our family through surrogacy. We’d naively thought what awaited us would be easier than the road that led there. Our experiences with surrogacy have changed how we show up for each other, both in joy and in grief.

I can’t say for certain that our marriage is now strong enough to survive anything that lies ahead. What I know is this: We’ve built what we’ll need to recalibrate our direction to find each other in the dark.

How to Use Jojoba Oil for Hair: Expert Tips for Stunning Results

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.
  • The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds.
  • Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

It has been revealed that “Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” states Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo claims it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

It has been revealed that while its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”.

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo states, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”.

She claims adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo notes she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:.

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she says can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”.

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets states that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

#68566. "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1290 w)

"All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the newly introduced Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.
  • Sources indicate that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes.
  • Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the newly introduced Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the newly introduced Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

Sources indicate that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the newly introduced Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks.

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sources indicate that sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

That last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

It has been revealed that nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the massive deal.

A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Industry observers note that that is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

Sources indicate that the architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same complications that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility concerns – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many customers, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Brooklyn Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers.

It has been revealed that that leaves only a deeper glitch, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

In a recent development, objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once stated, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

Tech Report: Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.
  • The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
  • It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum demonstrates today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

It has been revealed that with The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh states, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused Latest Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the concerns that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

According to recent reports, “I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”.

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

It has been revealed that next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she claims has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she said.

It has been revealed that the Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

6 Signs Your Skin Needs Medical Attention, Stat

📅 12 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off.
  • Many of these skin issues get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine.
  • According to recent reports, but if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin complications from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

Many of these skin issues get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

According to recent reports, but if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health issue.

Here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a plan of action.

If you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:.

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:.

Sources indicate that A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a latest outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

In a recent development, A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the glitch.

Dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:.

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

In a recent development, psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s key to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Industry observers note that changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin problems, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

Recent findings suggest that the good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

According to recent reports, no one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically demonstrates up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

Recent findings suggest that common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

An irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:.

In a recent development, these types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

Industry observers note that skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying glitch that needs to be addressed.

It has been revealed that A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment proposal to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t right now have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.
